## Discussion

By systematically re-mining public human RNA-seq, recovering the non-human reads that standard transcriptomic pipelines discard, we resolved the productive status of cutaneous HPV across the spectrum from healthy skin to carcinoma, while controlling for the two confounders that have dogged this question: laboratory contamination and sequencing depth. Three findings stand out. First, HPV signal in archived RNA-seq is dominated by cell-line and engineered material and by the integrated mucosal types HPV16/HPV18, so that genuine primary skin carries HPV at only 2–4%. Second, and centrally, HPV in cutaneous neoplasia (cSCC/AK) is present only as a transcriptionally inactive trace, not as productive infection, and this gap is not an artifact of how deeply the libraries were sequenced. Third, the same assay readily detects productive infection where it genuinely occurs: in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV), and in a minority of bona fide primary-skin lesions carrying beta- and alpha-HPV.

### Trace, not productive: the transcriptomic phenotype of cutaneous neoplasia

The defining prediction of the "hit-and-run" hypothesis is that beta-HPV acts early in cutaneous carcinogenesis but is dispensable for tumour maintenance, so that viral load and transcription decline as lesions progress and are minimal or absent in established carcinoma [@howley2015]. The experimental backbone of this model is genetic: in transgenic and infection systems, deleting the viral oncogenes after lesions have formed, or transplanting secondary tumours, leaves carcinoma growth unaffected and viral genomes undetectable [@viarisio2018; @dorfer2021], and in human tissue viral load and transcription are highest in early precursor lesions and fall in established tumours [@borgogna2018]. Our data provide a complementary, population-scale transcriptomic read-out of the same prediction. Across `r comma(stats$neo_n)` cSCC/AK libraries, only `r stats$neo_pos_floor` reached the control-calibrated detection floor (`r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor)`%), against `r pp(stats$ctrl_pctfloor)`% of productive controls, and the group's median burden was `r formatC(stats$neo_medrpm, format="f", digits=3)` RPM against `r comma(stats$ctrl_medrpm)` RPM in controls. Neoplasia does carry HPV more often than clean skin, both as a trace signal (any read; OR `r fo(stats$m2a_or)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2a_p)`) and, marginally, at the detection floor (OR `r fo(stats$m2b_or)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2b_p)`; halved to OR `r fo(stats$m2b_or_cut)` once the `r stats$cin_n` mucosal HPV16 cases are removed). But that elevation is a rise from near-zero to near-zero, and it is not converted into productive burden by any amount of sequencing. This is the residual footprint, rather than active infection, that hit-and-run predicts. It is not, however, evidence for that model over its competitors, for reasons set out below. This is not a new observation, and we do not present it as one. Transcriptional silence of HPV in cutaneous carcinoma has now been reported from four independent RNA-sequencing series: the original cSCC transcriptome study [@arron2011], total RNA sequencing of skin lesions at a median 66 million reads [@hultin2019], whole-transcriptome analysis of 345 post-transplant non-melanoma skin cancers at a median 35 million reads with transcription in 15 [@arroyomuhr2021], and RNA sequencing of 23 risk-stratified cSCC biopsies with no HPV expression against 64% DNA positivity in the same samples [@vandiver2021], the DNA-present/RNA-absent dissociation we report here with the paired modality our design cannot supply. An orthogonal assay agrees at comparable cohort size: E6/E7 mRNA in situ hybridization across 243 cutaneous SCC detected high-risk transcripts in 0.9% of the 225 non-anogenital cases [@fujimoto2019]. Two of the sequencing series ran at medians of 35 and 66 million reads, and so had already disposed of the possibility that this negative is an artifact of shallow sequencing. Nor is the literature unanimous: in situ hybridization on PCR-positive transplant-recipient cSCC demonstrated EV-HPV transcripts in 4 of 11 tumours, localized to the mid and upper epidermis [@purdie2005], a focal, suprabasal signal that bulk sequencing of a whole biopsy averages away and that our design would not recover.

What our data add is not the direction of the result but its denominator, its controls and its criterion. The prior transcriptomic series run from 11 to 345 specimens; ours covers `r comma(stats$neo_n)` cSCC/AK libraries against `r comma(stats$uns_n)` unselected-skin libraries in the same pipeline, which converts an absence reported within lesions into a case/control contrast with an estimated effect size. The largest prior series is confined to formalin-fixed material from transplant recipients; ours is restricted to neither, so the result is not conditional on immunosuppression or on archival fixation. And where the prior work scores HPV presence or transcription, we score productive replication from late capsid transcripts against a floor calibrated on lesions in which productive infection is certain, so that "no productive infection in cSCC/AK" is measured on the same instrument that reports `r pp(stats$ctrl_pctfloor)`% productivity in warts rather than asserted from a null result. The depth argument likewise changes role: it is no longer the discovery that depth was not the explanation, which @arroyomuhr2021 had already established, but a modeled covariate across that contrast, and the neoplasia libraries were in any case sequenced almost four times more deeply than the productive controls (median `r mreads(stats$neo_medreads)` vs `r mreads(stats$ctrl_medreads)` reads), with even the deepest, at `r p1(stats$neo_maxreads)`M reads, not crossing the productive threshold.

That said, transcriptomic absence cannot by itself adjudicate the mechanism, and the reason is sharper than a general appeal to correlation. The decline of viral activity from healthy skin to carcinoma is not the discriminating observation it was once taken to be, because all three live accounts predict it.

Under hit-and-run, activity falls because the virus is dispensable once the tumour is established [@howley2015; @viarisio2018; @dorfer2021]. Under the protective-immunity account, it falls because virus-positive cells are selected against: the original report already showed reduced beta-HPV activity and load in human skin cancer relative to adjacent healthy skin [@strickley2019], and the mechanism has since been resolved further, with papillomavirus colonization blocking the expansion of mutant p53 clones in a CD8^+^ T-cell-dependent manner, beta-HPV activity elevated in sun-exposed human skin bearing such clones, and clonal expansion in premalignant lesions associated with loss of beta-HPV [@son2025]. A falling viral signal along the progression axis is therefore a shared prediction, and our data, which measure exactly that axis, cannot separate the two. That work also reports beta-HPV activity *elevated* in sun-exposed human skin, which sits in apparent tension with the quiet reservoir we describe. The two measurements are not commensurate: theirs is in situ viral activity in the epidermis, localized to keratinocyte clones in UV-damaged skin, whereas ours is a whole-biopsy bulk average over archived libraries with no stratification by UV exposure, and a focal signal confined to a small clonal compartment is precisely what such an average dilutes. Our healthy-skin figure should therefore be read as a population-level transcript abundance in unselected skin, not as a claim that no keratinocyte anywhere is transcribing beta-HPV. We note also that the protective-immunity claim is itself contested in the primary literature, having drawn a Matters Arising and a reply in the same journal [@lambert2021; @strickley2021], so presenting it as one settled half of a two-way contest would misdescribe the field.

A third account requires no oncogenic or immunological premise at all. The beta-HPV genome restricts its own gene expression and replication through the viral E8\^E2 protein, and immortalization of human keratinocytes by a beta-HPV genome requires that repressor to be inactivated as well as E6, E7, E1 and E2 to be present [@rehm2022]. On that reading, a transcriptionally quiet beta-HPV genome in skin is the virus in its default state, and quiescence carries no information about oncogenic mechanism whatsoever. Our observation that the cutaneous reservoir is episomal and quiet in healthy skin, and remains quiet in neoplasia, is consistent with this without requiring it.

What our data therefore establish is not a verdict between models but the phenomenology all of them must accommodate, measured rather than assumed: established cutaneous neoplasia does not host productive HPV infection. `r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor)`% of cSCC/AK libraries reach the productive floor, against `r pp(stats$ctrl_pctfloor)`% of lesions in which productive infection is certain, and that gap is independent of sequencing depth and of library chemistry. Our cross-sectional snapshot of bulk transcription measures viral activity, not causation, and cannot distinguish a virus that has "hit and run" from one that was selected against by immunity, or from one that was never transcriptionally active to begin with.

One line of evidence does go beyond observation, and it is worth stating precisely what it shows. In a double-blind randomized sham-controlled trial, 70 immunocompetent adults with 15 or more actinic keratoses received a nine-valent papillomavirus vaccine or sham. Lesion-burden reductions were greater in the vaccinated group at 6 and 12 months (47% versus 29%, *P* = 0.01; 58% versus 47%, *P* = 0.05), with fewer thick lesions, and no difference in the rate of new lesions or in keratinocyte-carcinoma incidence over the year [@wenande2025]. This is the interventional experiment a cross-sectional transcriptomic survey cannot perform, and it shows that manipulating papillomavirus immunity changes precancerous lesion burden. It is not evidence that beta-HPV is productively replicating in those lesions, and it does not identify the virus responsible: the vaccine targets nine mucosal alphapapillomavirus types, none of them the cutaneous beta-types that dominate the skin reservoir, so any effect must run through cross-reactive or non-specific immunity rather than through neutralizing the resident virus. Our result is consistent with that reading rather than in tension with it, since an immunological intervention can reduce lesion burden without productive viral replication being present to target.

### Productive cutaneous HPV is real, but it is the property of warts and EV

The trace-level neoplasia result is not a failure of sensitivity. The assay recovered abundant productive infection in the positive-control lesions: `r round(stats$m3_ctrl_pct)`% of targeted wart/EV libraries met the strict L1 major-capsid criterion, spanning the expected cutaneous repertoire (HPV2/27/57, HPV6/11, and diverse beta/gamma types), consistent with the differentiation-coupled late program that defines productive papillomavirus infection [@doorbar2012; @egawa2017]. The contrast between productive controls and neoplasia was significant (OR `r fo(stats$m3_or)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m3_p)`). A small number of genuine, non-cell-line skin lesions also harbored unambiguous productive infection, most strikingly an HPV12-productive cSCC and two lesions co-infected with the beta types HPV96 and HPV182 at near-complete genome coverage and high depth. These cases matter for two reasons. They confirm that bona fide productive cutaneous beta/gamma infection occurs in primary tissue and can be detected from public RNA-seq, which answers the original descriptive question about productive infection. The companion question about non-traditional tissues is not answered here: every one of these libraries is cutaneous, and the residual group that would have to supply non-cutaneous evidence is defined by missing site metadata rather than by an identified site elsewhere, so this design can bound HPV activity in skin but cannot survey the tissues outside it. They also show that the population-level "trace" conclusion is a statement about the central tendency of cSCC/AK, not a claim that productive cutaneous HPV disease never exists. The picture that emerges aligns with the commensal model of cutaneous HPV [@antonsson2000; @foulongne2012]: a ubiquitous but transcriptionally quiet beta/gamma reservoir in normal skin, overt productive disease confined to warts and EV, and only a residual footprint in carcinoma.

### What a 2-4% transcriptome prevalence means against a 90% DNA reservoir

Our primary-skin figure of 2-4% sits against a DNA literature reporting cutaneous beta-HPV in the large majority of healthy adults, and the gap is wide enough that it has to be addressed directly rather than filed under limitations. It is not a contradiction, because the two numbers measure different things, and three published quantities show why.

The first is abundance. Quantitative PCR of eyebrow hair follicles across 782 immunocompetent people and organ-transplant recipients found median beta-HPV DNA loads below one viral copy per 60 cells, spanning seven orders of magnitude [@weissenborn2012]. A commensal carried at that density is below the detection floor of bulk RNA sequencing by construction: even under perfect transcription, one genome per 60 cells contributes a vanishing fraction of a library's reads. Most of the DNA assays reporting high prevalence are type-specific PCR amplifications designed to find exactly this, and they are orders of magnitude more sensitive than untargeted sequencing of total RNA; the untargeted metagenomic survey that also reports high skin prevalence sampled skin-surface sites [@ma2014], which brings in the second difference.

The second is substrate. The standard substrates of cutaneous beta-HPV epidemiology are surface skin swabs and plucked eyebrow hair bulbs, and the choice between them changes the answer: in the same 370 individuals, beta-HPV prevalence was 92% in swabs against 73% in eyebrow hairs, and gamma-HPV 84% against 43% [@rollison2019sites]. Both sample the follicular and superficial compartments where the commensal reservoir resides. Our substrate is neither. Archived RNA-seq libraries are made from biopsy or excision tissue, which is dominated by the dermis and the viable epidermis and largely excludes the surface and follicular material that swabs and hair bulbs are designed to capture. Our 2-4% is therefore a statement about papillomavirus transcript abundance within intra-epidermal biopsy tissue, not an estimate of the reservoir as the DNA literature defines and samples it.

The third is the reference panel. Deep sequencing of human skin has cataloged 396 HPV types, of which 229 were previously unknown [@bzhalava2014], whereas typing here is anchored on the PaVE reference set of `r stats$panel_n` sequences. Types with no reference genome cannot be assigned by any panel-based method, so our prevalence is a floor with respect to cutaneous diversity as well as to abundance, and the trace-level detections that resolve to a confident type (@supptbl-trace) are the visible edge of a wider reservoir rather than its full extent.

Read together, these place the 2-4% where it belongs: as the transcriptionally detectable fraction of a reservoir that is genuinely near-ubiquitous at DNA level, and not as a competing prevalence estimate. That distinction matters beyond bookkeeping, because it is the same distinction the paper draws for neoplasia. Prospective work makes the point from the DNA side: among 1,008 individuals followed after baseline skin-swab typing, beta-HPV detection predicted subsequent cutaneous SCC, yet fewer than 5% of the beta-HPV types found on a person's skin were present in the tumour that person later developed [@rollison2021]. A second cohort, in a different population and with paired sampling by site, reaches the same conclusion: across 193 samples from organ-transplant recipients and immunocompetent patients with cSCC, 65 HPV genotypes were recovered, 56 of them from eyebrow hair against 30 from the carcinomas, and genotype-specific concordance between a patient's eyebrow hair and their own cSCC was found in 5 of 55 patients (9.1%) [@oh2026]. The commensal reservoir is richer than the tumour and largely not the same virus, which is what our transcriptomic data show at population scale and from the activity side.

### Actinic keratosis, HPV8, and what a bulk transcriptome cannot see

The precursor end of the neoplasia group deserves separate treatment, because a specific hit-and-run mechanism has been built on it. In mouse models, the HPV8 E6 protein binds p300 and phosphorylates STAT3, inducing ΔNp63 and driving proliferation and expansion of Lrig1^+^ hair-follicle junctional-zone keratinocyte stem cells into the overlying epidermis; HPV8 was reported in association with 70% of human actinic keratoses, and the authors frame the expansion of these melanosome-poor, UV-vulnerable stem cells as the hit-and-run mechanism itself [@morgan2024].

On presence, we do not disagree. Trace HPV reads were recovered from `r pp(stats$ak_pctany)`% of our `r stats$ak_n` AK libraries, which is the same order as their 70% association figure. Our result concerns what that material is doing, and the answer is the same in AK as in carcinoma: `r stats$ak_floor` of `r stats$ak_n` AK libraries reached the productive floor.

That is not a contradiction of their model, and is closer to a corroboration of it. A mechanism driven by E6 acting on a stem-cell compartment requires viral oncogene function, not capsid production, and a hit-and-run account predicts precisely that the virus leaves no productive footprint in the lesion it helped initiate. Our data supply the population-scale version of that prediction and find it satisfied.

Two things we cannot settle are worth stating plainly. The first is type. We detected no HPV8 anywhere in the cohort: no library met the assignment criterion for it, and it was the best-hit reference in none of the `r comma(stats$trace_libs)` trace-level libraries, although HPV8 is present in the reference panel and other beta-1 types including HPV5 and HPV12 were recovered. Whether that reflects genuine absence of HPV8 transcription, cohort composition, or the fact that DNA association and transcript detection need not coincide, we cannot determine from RNA alone. The DNA side of the same question is not silent, which sharpens rather than resolves it: the independent metagenome catalog places HPV8 in `r rv("hpv8_dna")` of `r comma(rvn("n_skin_lib"))` HPV-positive skin libraries, the eighth commonest type in that reservoir (@fig-reservoir A), against `r rv("hpv8_rna_all")` detections at any level here. The type most often named as the cutaneous carcinoma candidate is thus present on skin and, in this cohort, never transcribed above the detection floor. The second is compartment. The Lrig1^+^ junctional zone is a follicular structure, and it is exactly the compartment that our substrate under-samples: it is what plucked eyebrow-hair-bulb assays are designed to capture and what an excision biopsy dominated by dermis and interfollicular epidermis dilutes. A focal, follicular, stem-cell-restricted reservoir is the case our design is least able to see, and the negative we report for AK should be read with that limit attached.

### Contamination is the dominant signal in naïve analyses

Our cell-line finding is both a result and a methodological warning. The roughly five-fold enrichment of HPV positivity in cell-line and engineered libraries, dominated by HPV16/HPV18, mirrors the documented contamination of public sequence archives by HeLa-derived and other integrated-HPV reads [@adey2013; @cantalupo2015; @kazemian2015]. Where that contamination has been traced to its source, the mechanism is exactly the one our enrichment implies: applying a virus-detection workflow to 9,143 TCGA RNA-seq libraries from a single sequencing center attributed the HeLa-derived HPV18 signal, and a co-occurring XMRV signal, to a pool of cell lines run alongside the tumours as a quality-control reference, so that the tumours carrying those reads were not infected at all [@selitsky2020]. Our result is the same phenomenon at the scale of the whole archive rather than one center, and without the laboratory metadata that allowed that study to name the culprit. Nor is the problem confined to cell lines: systematically sequencing the laboratory components themselves showed that more than 65% of viral sequences recovered from 712 libraries fell into clusters linked to a reagent or protocol step rather than to the specimen [@asplund2019], which is why a detection floor calibrated on genuine productive lesions, rather than on the absence of reads, is doing necessary work here. Any survey that pools archived data without flagging non-primary material and without coverage-breadth and depth thresholds will substantially overstate HPV prevalence and mis-attribute mucosal high-risk types to tissues where they have no biological place. The cost of getting this wrong at archive scale is not hypothetical: re-analysis of the reported pan-cancer microbiome found that most of the microbes originally called were not present in the samples at all, invalidating the original report and more than a dozen studies built on it [@gihawi2023]. None of the individual safeguards we applied is novel, and the requirements have been set out before in reviews of virus detection in sequence data [@cantalupo2019]. What we contribute is their operationalization and measurement on one cohort: explicit cell-line, engineered and in-vitro annotation, study-level curation, dual breadth-and-depth typing thresholds, a control-calibrated productivity floor, and burden normalized for both depth and library chemistry, with the size of the artifact each is guarding against reported rather than asserted. That combination generalizes beyond HPV.

### What the integration marker measures

Reading integration from the relative abundance of viral genes is not new, and the marker used here should be located against that work rather than presented as an invention. In cervical disease, the ratio of E2 to E6 is an established surrogate for physical integration status: measured on cytology specimens from 226 HPV16-positive women it falls with lesion grade, from 0.79 in both normal epithelium and CIN1 to 0.48 in CIN2/3 and 0.36 in carcinoma, discriminating CIN2 or worse with an area under the curve of 0.844, and it declines alongside L1 capsid immunoreactivity [@choi2018]. The underlying biology, that the integrated fraction rises with lesion severity, is older still [@cheung2008]. The step from DNA ratios to transcript ratios has also been taken: integration status in head and neck squamous carcinoma has been classified from spliced virus-host fusion transcripts and from ratios of HPV gene transcripts across 261 RNA-seq samples in five cohorts, with DNA integration events in 102 participants as ground truth [@li2026]. The more general move, grading integration by its transcriptional output rather than its presence, is also established: in cervical cancer, integration sites that generate fusion transcripts behave differently from silent ones, and the productive fraction rises from carcinoma in situ to advanced disease [@fan2023]. Our cervical validation series reproduces that direction from a different measurement, which is a point in its favor rather than a novelty claim. What is specific to this study is narrower than the concept: an E1 numerator against an E2 denominator taken from bulk RNA-seq read counts, applied to cutaneous beta- and gamma-types in skin, and used as a provenance check rather than a clinical classifier. Even so, a marker that only ever fired on cultured cells would be indistinguishable from the metadata-based flagging it was meant to check independently. The graded cervical series settles that question in the direction that matters. Across HPV16-positive normal epithelium, high-grade lesion and carcinoma, sequenced under one protocol and labeled by the submitting study, the ratio moves monotonically with grade in primary tissue with no cell line anywhere in the series, and late transcription falls away along the same axis. The marker is therefore reading integration as a biological process rather than culture as a provenance, which is what licenses its use on skin: when it reports the cutaneous reservoir as episomal and quiet, that is a statement about the virus, not an echo of how the libraries were annotated. The series is small, and the normal-epithelium arm in particular rests on few informative libraries, so it establishes the direction of the marker rather than a calibrated scale. A second and more consequential limit comes from the cervical literature that established the ratio in the first place. An E2 deficit is not specific to advanced disease: triplex quantitative PCR for E6, E2 and beta-globin indicated integration in 44.3% of histologically negative control samples in a series of 380 women, with substantial overlap between cases and controls that precluded any usable cutoff [@boulet2009], and serial sampling of women recruited soon after first intercourse showed E2 disruption to be a common and early event in incident infection, occurring within months and more often for HPV18 than HPV16 [@collins2009]. Our inferential chain runs from a high E1:E2 to an episomal reservoir, and that chain is only as strong as the specificity of the deficit it inverts. One difference works in our favor without settling the matter: those studies measure DNA copy-number ratios, in which a minor integrated subclone can depress the ratio while the bulk population remains episomal, whereas we measure transcript ratios, which report what the viral population is actually expressing. Whether that makes the transcript form less susceptible to the early-integration confound is a reasonable expectation rather than something demonstrated here, and until it is tested the marker should be read as evidence about the dominant transcriptional state of the reservoir, not as a proof that no integrated genome is present. It is also worth being explicit about what the cervical data are not doing here. They are not a matched mucosal counterpart to the skin cohort, and the two are not contrasted quantitatively: the comparison that carries weight is within the cervical progression itself, where the confounders that separate any two archived cohorts, depth, protocol, selection and provenance, are held constant by design.

### What a petabase catalog does and does not measure

The DNA axis used here is a catalog, and catalogs answer a narrower question than they appear to. The Logan-wide papillomavirus survey identifies contigs by profile-HMM filtering with identification of the conserved L1 B and I domains [@shenpv2026], over an assembly of 27 million archived sequencing libraries [@chikhi2024], so a contig enters the catalog because it carries a detectable L1. Three consequences follow, and together they bound what any comparison against such a resource can claim. First, presence in the catalog means L1-detectable presence, and carries no information about the state of the viral genome. Second, the catalog is assembly-based, and an integrated genome cannot assemble across the virus-host junction, so integrated molecules are systematically under-recovered: conditioning on near-complete contigs returns an intact E2 in 99.3% of cervical carcinoma contigs against 99.9% in skin (@supptbl-e2), which is close to a tautology rather than a biological result, because the completeness criterion has already selected episomal genomes in both. Third, because every contig is anchored on L1 and extends outward from it, the frequency with which an open reading frame is truncated at a contig terminus tracks its distance from that anchor rather than the position of any breakpoint; the ordering E1 > E2 > L1 holds in every body site examined, including healthy vaginal and gut carriage, where integration cannot explain it. Genome state therefore has to be read from reads or from transcription rather than from catalog membership, which is what the E1:E2 ratio and the virus-host junctions do above. The point generalizes beyond papillomaviruses: petabase-scale surveys are now the standard way to establish that a virus is present in a body site, and a presence count from such a survey is not evidence of an active infection. Within those bounds the catalog is exactly the right instrument for the one job it is given here. Read as presence and nothing more, it establishes independently of our pipeline, our modality and our cohort that the cutaneous beta/gamma reservoir this survey reports as quiet is really there, in the expected genera and the expected types (@fig-reservoir), so the negative result is a statement about activity rather than about whether the virus was present to be transcribed. The two arms nonetheless sample different compartments, surface swabs against bulk tissue, as set out above; that difference bounds any quantitative comparison between them, which is why the reservoir is used here as corroboration of presence and never as a denominator for the transcriptional rate.

### Strengths and limitations

The principal strengths of this work are its scale, its uniform end-to-end processing of heterogeneous public data, and its explicit control of the depth, chemistry and contamination confounders that limit prior reports. Recovering discarded non-human reads turns a vast existing resource toward a question it was never collected to answer [@edgar2022], and reading productivity directly from the early/late transcript program provides a biologically grounded activity measure rather than mere presence/absence. That last point is where this work sits relative to the two prior archive-scale mining studies of skin. Screening off-target reads across 19 skin tumour types was a search for a driver, and found one, in an acral tumour outside the beta-HPV question entirely [@leiendecker2023]; reprocessing 8,274 public skin libraries cataloged HPV among the foreign RNA of skin without typing it, scoring its productivity or setting it against a case/control design [@bhargava2025]. Both establish that the substrate is rich. Neither asks, and neither can answer, at what rate cutaneous HPV is transcribed across the spectrum from healthy skin to carcinoma and whether that transcription is productive, which is the question this study is built around.

Several limitations temper interpretation. First, the unbiased prevalence sweep screened `r comma(stats$n_screened)` libraries, a large but not exhaustive sample of public human skin RNA-seq: of roughly 12,200 candidate runs discovered, the remainder were lost to withdrawn accessions, download failures or quality-control exclusion, and archival sampling is itself non-random, so the absolute healthy-skin positivity rate is best read as an estimate. Second, library-selection chemistry biases viral recovery, and although we measured it rather than assuming it away, we could not measure it everywhere. Chemistry was resolvable for `r pp(stats$chem_pct)`% of libraries; for the remainder the SRA record and the submitted protocol text are both silent, and those libraries carry the trace signal alongside the resolved ones. Where it is known, the axis of concern is flat: rRNA-depleted libraries were no more likely than poly-A libraries to carry an HPV read at equal depth (OR `r fo(stats$chem_ribo_or)`, `r oci(stats$chem_ribo_lo, stats$chem_ribo_hi)`), and the group reported here as non-productive is the one more often built with the favorable chemistry. What this does not settle is the rest of library construction. Selection chemistry is only one axis: input amount, RNA integrity and fragment-size selection are not recoverable from archived metadata at all, and a poly-A-selected library remains, in principle, a conservative instrument for late viral transcripts. Absence of HPV reads is therefore not proof of absence of virus, and our productivity estimates remain conservative. Third, bulk sequencing of a whole biopsy averages over every cell in it, so transcription confined to a small, focal cell fraction is diluted below detection. This is not hypothetical for cutaneous HPV: in situ hybridization localizes EV-HPV transcripts to the mid and upper epidermal layers of cSCC [@purdie2005], precisely the spatially restricted, suprabasal pattern that a whole-biopsy average is least able to see. Our productivity estimates are therefore a lower bound on focal transcription, and the negative we report is a statement about population-level viral burden rather than about every cell in every tumour. Fourth, tissue and diagnosis labels were derived programmatically from sample metadata and are imperfect, despite curation; residual misclassification adds noise to the group assignments. Fifth, typing is anchored on a fixed reference panel, and deep sequencing of skin has described 229 HPV types that had no reference genome at the time of that survey [@bzhalava2014]; such types are invisible to any panel-based assignment, so our type catalog and prevalence are bounded by the panel as well as by detection sensitivity. Sixth, the high sequence similarity among HPV types permits cross-mapping, which we mitigated with breadth/depth thresholds and multimapping-aware alignment but cannot wholly exclude; the same caveat attaches to distinguishing low-level true infection from residual contaminant signal at the detection floor, although the transcripts themselves bound the problem: decomposing the below-floor libraries by gene shows that `r tr("trace_pct_nogene")`% carry no reads on any HPV gene and are best read as a k-mer and cross-mapping floor, while a minority carry early-gene transcripts without the late programme, the signature of latent or abortive infection, on cutaneous rather than mucosal types (@suppfig-trace). The sub-threshold trace is therefore neither wholly artifactual nor productive. Seventh, our data are transcriptomic and cross-sectional: we cannot observe viral DNA persistence, integration state, or the temporal decline in viral activity that the hit-and-run model specifies, and we therefore describe the productive-status phenomenology rather than prove the mechanism. Finally, the L1-based productivity rule, while deliberately stringent, depends on beta/gamma gene annotation quality and treats integrated-line L1 signal cautiously (reported only in the supplement).

### Conclusion

Mining the reads that transcriptomic studies routinely throw away, we find that the cutaneous HPV reservoir of healthy skin is real but transcriptionally quiet, that productive cutaneous HPV infection is the property of warts and EV, and that HPV in cutaneous squamous neoplasia, at population scale and independent of both sequencing depth and library chemistry, is a trace, non-productive footprint rather than an active infection. This transcriptomic phenotype is the common ground that every current account of beta-HPV in skin cancer must explain, whether the virus is a departed cofactor, the target of protective immunity, or a genome that is transcriptionally restricted by default. Because a declining viral signal is predicted by all three, separating them will not be achieved by measuring viral activity more precisely. It will require designs that break the shared prediction: matched DNA- and RNA-level profiling across the precursor-to-carcinoma transition, resolution of where the residual virus resides relative to mutant clones and to infiltrating T cells, linkage to host antiviral immunity in the same tissue, and interventional studies of the kind the VAXAK trial has now begun [@wenande2025]. The single-cell assay is not itself the missing piece: HPV transcripts have already been resolved to basal keratinocytes, suprabasal keratinocytes and hair-follicle stem cells within a cutaneous lesion by single-cell RNA sequencing [@devitt2019]. What has not been done is to apply it at cohort scale across the actinic-keratosis-to-carcinoma transition in beta- and gamma-positive lesions, which is where a shared prediction of declining activity would finally come apart into distinguishable ones. The public-archive mining framework developed here, with its contamination controls and its normalization for both depth and library chemistry, provides a scalable foundation for identifying the cohorts worth taking to that resolution.
